short.headline: India's New Climate Normal
short.dek: Hotter nights, stickier heat, sharper rain and unequal cooling are already changing daily life.
short.body: India has warmed, but the real story is not one national temperature line. ERA5 shows warmer decades, many more warm nights, more humid-heat days and heavier clustered rain. January-May 2026 is hot and dry so far, but not a full-year verdict. Climate risk now runs through sleep, work, farming, water, air, power bills and who can afford to cool a room.

macha.heading: Okay, what changes for me?
macha.body: Think less "one more hot day" and more "less recovery". The day is hotter, the night cools less, sweat works worse when the air is humid, and rain can arrive in harder bursts. If you work outside, farm, live in a hot room, pay the power bill, depend on groundwater or buy vegetables after a bad monsoon, climate change is already in the routine.
macha.soWhat: The average Indian climate is shifting, but the cost lands hardest where work is outdoors, homes are hotter and cooling is expensive.

article.title: How Climate Change Is Rewriting Everyday India
article.standfirst: India's climate story is no longer just a warmer average. It is hotter nights, humid body stress, heavier rain spells, stretched water buffers, exposed work and unequal cooling.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## Is India actually hotter now?

Yes. In ERA5, India went from about 1 degree cooler than the 1991-2020 normal in 1940 to slightly warmer than that normal in 2025. The hottest recent point was 2016, about 0.7 degrees above the recent normal, and the 2016-2025 decade averaged roughly a third of a degree above it. That sounds small only if you read it like the temperature outside your window. It is not. A national annual anomaly spreads extra heat across a huge landmass and every season. The average is also polite. It smooths Delhi's May afternoon, a Chennai night that will not cool, a tin-roof room in Nagpur and a field in Telangana into one line. The line answers the first question: the baseline has moved. The rest of the article is about where that movement hurts.

## Is this just one dataset?

No. ERA5 is the main workhorse in this article because it gives India-wide hourly heat, humidity and rainfall metrics through 2025. But the basic warming story does not depend on ERA5 alone. When ERA5, OWID/Copernicus and Berkeley Earth are put on the same 1991-2020 baseline, the year-to-year lines differ because the products use different methods, land masks and source data. The direction is the point: older decades sit lower, recent decades sit higher. That matters because a common objection is to attack one source or one hot year. The fair test is whether independent temperature products tell the same broad story. They do.

## Is India warming slower than everyone else?

India is not the fastest-warming country in this selected comparison. That is true, and it is also not the argument people think it is. In the OWID/Copernicus series, India's 2016-2025 decade is about 0.97°C warmer than its 1940s average; the world is about 1.10°C warmer on the same calculation, Bangladesh about 0.99°C, China about 1.23°C and the United States about 2.10°C. So the honest line is: India has warmed roughly as much as the world, not uniquely fastest and not untouched. Also, this is degrees Celsius, not percent. A one-degree shift in a national annual average is a big physical change when it lands on a hot, humid, densely populated country where many people work outdoors and sleep without reliable cooling.

## Which region has warmed fastest?

The national line hides a rougher map. The Himalayan belt has warmed far faster than the all-India average in this ERA5 regional split, while the Indo-Gangetic plain, the arid west, the Deccan and the peninsula have their own rhythms. That does not mean the mountains are the only danger zone. High warming in a sparse mountain belt matters for snow, glaciers, springs and downstream water. Smaller annual-average warming in the plains can still mean brutal heat exposure because so many people live and work there. Averages by region are useful because they stop the lazy national story. They are still averages. A farmer near Akola, a delivery rider in Lucknow and a tea worker in Assam do not experience one Indian climate.

## Where does the state map change the story?

The state map makes the same point in political geography. States are not climate zones, but they are where heat action plans, school closures, power supply and disaster relief get administered. A national average cannot tell a state government whether its problem is hot nights, dry pre-monsoon heat, humid coastal heat or flood bursts. The map also warns against a simple north-versus-south reading. Mountain states can show high warming because cold places warm fast in average-temperature terms. Dense plains can carry larger human exposure even when the colour is less dramatic. This is why a canonical India climate article cannot stop at one all-India line. The lived question is local: what kind of heat, rain and coping capacity lands where people are?

## Why does the pre-monsoon window matter so much?

March to May is the dangerous waiting room before the monsoon. In the ERA5 pre-monsoon series, the 2016-2025 decade averaged about a quarter of a degree above the 1991-2020 normal, while the 1980s were about 0.3 degrees below it. The peak years are much hotter than that average. This season is when construction sites shift timings, schools debate closures, reservoirs are drawn down and power demand climbs before rain brings relief. It is also why an annual-average chart can understate the social problem. A mild winter and a punishing April can average into a neat number. Bodies do not live annual averages. Crops and work shifts do not either.

## How hot is 2026 so far?

Through January-May, 2026 is hot, but the honest comparison is only against earlier January-May periods. In this ERA5 year-to-date series, all-India January-May 2026 is about 0.44 degrees above the 1991-2020 January-May normal. That ranks seventh warmest in the 1940-2026 comparable record, not first. The regional lines matter because the all-India number can hide where the pain sits in a given year. This is a warning box, not a verdict on the year. June to September can change the calendar-year rank, and the monsoon can change the water story. The right sentence is: 2026 began hot, and the first five months already sit high in the modern distribution.

## What happens when nights stop cooling?

Warm nights are the difference between a bad day and a bad week. In the hourly ERA5-derived series, all-India warm nights, when the regional daily minimum stays at or above 26°C, averaged about 47 nights a year in the 1980s. In 2016-2025, that average was roughly 74. The latest year, 2025, had about 68 such nights, down from the extreme 2024 peak but still far above the 1980s. This is the part of heat that a daytime maximum misses. A room, a body and a city need night-time cooling to recover. Without it, sleep breaks, illness risk rises, and people start the next workday already carrying yesterday's heat.

## Are 40°C days becoming more common everywhere?

The 40°C chart is a useful trap for the eye. The all-India line does not rise cleanly from left to right. It averaged about 18 hot days a year in the 1980s and about 19 in 2016-2025. In 2025 it was only about 13. That does not mean heat risk has eased. A 40°C dry-heat threshold is a blunt measure, and the national average dilutes the arid west and the northern plains. West and arid India still averaged about 41 such days in the latest decade, and 2010 crossed 60. Threshold charts are for exposure, not for proving the whole climate trend. Read them beside warm nights and humid heat, or they will mislead you.

## Why does humidity make heat more dangerous?

Humidity is the reason two 38°C days can feel completely different. Sweat cools the body only when it evaporates. When the air is wet, evaporation slows and the same thermometer reading becomes harder to survive. In the hourly ERA5-derived heat-index series, all-India humid-heat days at or above a 40°C heat index averaged about 42 days a year in the 1980s. In 2016-2025, the average was about 68. The south peninsula moved from roughly 22 to 48. This is one of the clearest lived-experience signals in the whole article. It connects climate to fainting at school assembly, slower outdoor work, more dangerous kitchens and nights where a fan moves hot damp air around the room.

## Is the monsoon getting more unstable?

The monsoon chart should not be read as a neat warming line. Rain is noisier than temperature. The all-India southwest monsoon anomaly swings hard from year to year, with 1987 deeply dry and 2025 well above the 1991-2020 normal in ERA5. The latest decade in this series was wetter than the 1980s on average, but that is not the comfort it first sounds like. India does not only need a seasonal total. It needs rain at the right time, over the right basin, at a rate soil, drains and reservoirs can handle. A normal or wet monsoon can still contain a failed sowing window, a city flood, or a reservoir that fills too late.

## Are rainy days changing?

Wet-day counts ask a simple question the seasonal-total chart cannot: is rain spread out across usable days? In the ERA5 hourly-derived all-India series, days with at least 1 mm of regional-average rain averaged about 114 in the 1980s and about 125 in 2016-2025. The regional lines do not move in perfect lockstep. That matters because agriculture, groundwater recharge and city drainage care about sequencing. Ten moderate rainy days are not the same as one violent burst followed by a dry spell, even if the monthly total looks similar. This chart is not a district rain calendar. It is a warning that the distribution of rain across days is part of the climate story, not a footnote.

## Where does heavy rain become a city problem?

Heavy-rain days translate climate into infrastructure. In the all-India ERA5 hourly-derived series, days above 50 mm averaged about 2.4 a year in the 1980s and about 2.8 in 2016-2025. The line is small because it is a regional average. Local cloudbursts are sharper than this. Still, the direction matters: a little more heavy rain on a regional average can mean a lot more water moving through drains, culverts, lake beds, railway underpasses and low-lying settlements. Flood risk is not only about the sky. It is also about concrete, encroached drains and whether a city has left water somewhere to go. The rain chart shows the physical pressure; the damage depends on the ground below it.

## Why is the wettest five-day spell worth watching?

The wettest five-day spell is a better flood signal than the annual total. In the all-India ERA5 hourly-derived series, the rainiest five-day stretch averaged about 159 mm in the 1980s and about 174 mm in 2016-2025. In 2024 it crossed 200 mm, and 2025 was still around 179 mm. This is the kind of clustering that tests dams, drains, slopes and crop fields. A farmer does not benefit from a month's rain falling in a few days. A city does not either. The annual maximum is jumpy by design, so do not worship one spike. But the decade comparison says clustered rain has become heavier enough to deserve its own chart.

## Why does the monsoon still dominate the water year?

Even with changing seasons, the southwest monsoon still carries most of India's annual rain. In the hourly-derived ERA5 series, June-September usually supplies roughly seven-tenths to four-fifths of the year's precipitation. The latest decade averaged about 74%, close to the 1980s but with plenty of annual variation. This concentration is why the monsoon is not just weather. It is the refill period for reservoirs, canals, groundwater, rainfed fields and city lakes. A delayed or badly distributed monsoon can create stress long before the annual total is known. A strong monsoon can also flood places that cannot absorb it. The share chart explains why four months can decide so much of the year.

## What does IMD's long record add?

ERA5 gives a gridded climate spine. IMD's long all-India monsoon record is the historical reality check. It runs back to 1901 and shows why Indians have always treated the monsoon as a risk, not a tap. The worst drought years are deep, and the wettest years are not automatically good news because rain can arrive in destructive bursts. The record also stops a common mistake: using one wet year to dismiss climate risk, or one dry year to claim permanent collapse. Monsoon rainfall has always been volatile. Climate change loads that volatility onto a warmer land surface, warmer nights, changed moisture and more exposed people. That combination is the problem.

## Is 2026 already a drought year?

No. It is too early to call 2026 a drought year from this chart. The ERA5 January-May precipitation anomaly is about 14% below the 1991-2020 January-May normal, placing it in the drier end of the comparable record. But January-May is not the southwest monsoon. A dry start can matter for soil moisture, reservoirs and pre-monsoon crops, and when it comes with above-normal heat it raises stress. It still does not settle June-September. This section exists because readers are right to ask about the current year. The answer has to be disciplined: 2026 began hot and relatively dry through May. The monsoon verdict is not in this data yet.

## Why does groundwater decide whether rain failure becomes pain?

Rainfall is the supply shock. Groundwater is the buffer. When the buffer is thin, a weak monsoon reaches farms, taps and tankers faster. The CGWB stage-of-extraction series compares annual groundwater extraction with the assessed rechargeable resource. Values near 100% mean the area is drawing close to what can be replenished; values above that mean extraction is beyond the assessed annual recharge. This is not a monthly aquifer gauge and it cannot tell you what every well is doing. But it explains why the same rainfall deficit is not the same event everywhere. A canal command area, a tubewell belt and a tanker-dependent suburb do not enter a dry year with equal protection.

## What does sea level add to the India story?

For coastal India, climate change is not only heat and rain. A higher sea raises the floor under storm surge, high tides and drainage failure. The Mumbai and Chennai tide-gauge records are not perfect national sea-level measures. They combine ocean change with local land movement, and the histories have gaps. But they give the right civic warning. A city that already floods in heavy rain has less room for error when the outfall sits against a higher tide. Coastal risk is a compound problem: heavier rain from above, a rising sea at the edge, and dense settlement in between. That is why a climate article about India needs one coastal chart, even if heat is the main thread.

## How much does the monsoon still guide the harvest?

Irrigation, procurement and better seeds have weakened the old drought-to-famine chain. They have not made the monsoon irrelevant. The crop correlation chart shows which outputs still move with monsoon rainfall in the historical panel. Foodgrains, rice and oilseeds track rainfall more than irrigated winter crops such as wheat. Correlation is not causation, and it is not a yield forecast. Crop output also depends on area, heat, pests, prices, procurement and seed choice. Still, the pattern is enough to reject a lazy urban view that the monsoon is now just nostalgia. For a large part of Indian agriculture, the rain still writes the first draft of the season.

## Which crops take the first hit?

The crop-yield stress test makes the food story more concrete. El Nino years are used here as weak-monsoon stress years, and each crop is compared with its own recent five-year normal. Rainfed kharif crops are more exposed than crops protected by irrigation or winter timing. That does not mean every El Nino year causes the same harvest loss. It means climate risk enters the food system unevenly. A rice farmer with groundwater in Punjab is not in the same position as a rainfed oilseed or pulse grower in a drier belt. The plate feels climate through these differences. So do farm incomes, rural wages and food bills months after the rainfall shock.

## Why do food prices spike unevenly?

Food inflation is not one object. Cereals, pulses, onions, vegetables, edible oils and milk sit inside different supply chains. The food WPI component chart uses selected El Nino drought years to show why a weak monsoon does not produce one clean price response. Public grain stocks can soften cereals while pulses or onions jump. Imports, export bans, procurement, storage and global prices can amplify or mute the rain signal. This is why climate is a cost-of-living story without being a one-cause inflation model. A household does not buy "food inflation". It buys tomatoes, dal, rice, milk and cooking oil. Climate shocks reach each item through a different pipe.

## How does dirty air fit into a climate article?

PM2.5 is not climate change. It is dirty air. But in India, the sources overlap enough that it belongs in the same lived-exposure story. Burning coal, diesel, biomass and industrial fuel warms the climate over time and dirties the air now, though the chemistry and health pathways differ. IQAir's annual country-average PM2.5 series falls from about 73 micrograms per cubic metre in 2018 to about 49 in 2025. That is movement in the right direction and still many times the World Health Organization's 5 microgram guideline. Treat this as recent monitor-network context, not a perfect exposure map. The point is simple: the fossil story is not only about 2100. It is in the lungs this year.

## Why are India's emissions still rising?

India's climate position is uncomfortable because two statements are true at once. The country is highly exposed to warming, and its annual CO2 emissions are still rising as electricity, transport, construction and industry grow. Development is energy-hungry. More homes want cooling, more factories need power, more cities move people and goods. The total-emissions chart is the scale chart, not the fairness chart. It tells you why India's choices matter to the future atmosphere. It does not tell you whether the average Indian has caused as much warming as the average American or Chinese person. For that, the next chart is the fairer lens. The article has to hold both without pretending one cancels the other.

## What is the fair per-person comparison?

Per-person emissions are the fairness check. India has a large and rising national total because 1.4 billion people add up. But the average Indian still emits far less CO2 each year than the average person in the United States, China, or many rich economies. This does not give India a free pass on future emissions. It does mean any honest global comparison must separate total scale from individual footprint and historical responsibility. A low per-person number also hides inequality inside India: an air-conditioned upper-income household and a rural household with one fan do not have the same footprint. Still, as a country comparison, per person is the lens that keeps population from masquerading as guilt.

## Where do the emissions come from?

The sector chart turns a moral argument into a work list. Electricity and heat, agriculture, manufacturing, transport, buildings, industry, waste and fugitive emissions are different problems. A coal power plant, paddy methane, a cement kiln and diesel freight do not have one solution. That is why a climate article needs sector composition after the total-emissions line. It stops the reader from imagining "emissions" as one pipe with one valve. The chart is not a policy ranking and not a claim that every tonne is equally easy to cut. It says where the tonnes sit. The political economy begins after that: who pays, what technology exists, what is reliable, and what poor households cannot afford to lose.

## Is coal still doing the work?

India's electricity transition is real and incomplete. Ember's generation data shows solar and wind rising from a small base, while coal still supplies the largest block of electricity. That matters because the same warming that raises cooling demand also pushes up power demand. If the extra demand is met mainly by coal, cooling becomes an adaptation that feeds the problem. If clean generation, storage, grids and demand management outrun demand growth, the loop weakens. Generation is the right chart here because capacity can flatter the story. A gigawatt of solar and a gigawatt of coal do not produce the same annual electricity. What matters for emissions and reliability is the power actually generated.

## Who can actually cool their home?

Heat becomes inequality when the escape route is expensive. The cooling-access series show that only a small minority of Indian households had an air conditioner in the latest survey snapshot, with urban ownership far above rural ownership. NFHS and NSS measures are not a perfect annual time series, and appliance markets move faster than surveys. Still, the gap is the point. A richer household can buy cooling, pay the bill and seal the room. A poorer household may rely on a fan, a cooler that fails in humid heat, a shaded courtyard, or simply endurance. Climate adaptation is already happening in India's homes. It is just not evenly available.

## Why doesn't the cooling map match the heat map?

Air coolers are common where dry heat makes them useful and cheaper than AC. They are much less useful in humid heat, where evaporation does not work well. That is why the cooler map should not be read as a simple protection map. High cooler ownership in dry states can still leave people exposed during very hot spells, and low ownership in humid states can reflect both poverty and the technology's limits. The map is useful because it shows adaptation as geography, not just income. People buy the cooling device that fits local climate and budget. Climate change is now testing both: more humid heat reduces the value of cheap cooling, while AC raises electricity demand and bills.

## Where is heat hardest to survive?

The vulnerability scatter joins three things that are often discussed separately: heat risk, lack of cooling protection and poverty. The dangerous corner is not simply the hottest state. It is the place where high heat exposure meets households without reliable cooling and less money to adapt. This is not a mortality model. It uses state-level context from different sources, so exact ranking would be fake precision. Its job is to stop a narrow climate reading. Heat risk is not only a weather hazard. It is housing material, work type, electricity reliability, savings, age, health and whether a family can change its routine without losing income. That is where climate becomes social inequality.

## Why does heat hit work before GDP?

India still has a large share of workers in agriculture and other vulnerable work. That exposure matters because heat first shows up as shorter work windows, slower pace, more breaks, higher illness risk and lost daily wages. GDP tables see some of that late, and some not at all. A salaried office worker with AC can shift hours or work indoors. A farm labourer, construction worker, street vendor or delivery rider has less control over the day. This chart is an exposure chart, not a measured damage chart. It tells us who is in the path of heat and rainfall disruption. The answer is a large part of India's workforce, especially people with the least bargaining power.

## How many work hours is heat already costing?

The Lancet Countdown labour-loss chart moves from exposure to estimated loss. In its India data sheet, agriculture accounts for about 66% of heat-related labour-hour losses and construction for about 20%. The underlying estimate is about 247 billion potential labour hours lost in 2024, not a payroll record and not a count of people absent from work. It is a modelled labour-capacity measure based on heat stress. Still, the sector split is hard to ignore. Heat damage falls on outdoor work first. For a daily-wage worker, a lost hour is not an abstract productivity statistic. It can be the difference between buying vegetables today or pushing the cost into tomorrow.

## Why do heat-death numbers disagree?

Heat mortality is where bad counting can become bad policy. Certified heatstroke deaths, disaster databases, surveillance reports and modelled excess deaths answer different questions. The small administrative counts depend on diagnosis, death certification and reporting channels. The large modelled estimates try to capture deaths that rise during heat even when the certificate does not say "heatstroke". Neither should be casually swapped for the other. The comparison chart is deliberately uncomfortable because it shows how definition-sensitive the toll is. The safest conclusion is not that one bar is the truth and the rest are wrong. It is that registered heatstroke deaths are almost certainly too narrow to describe the full health burden of extreme heat.

## How much more cooling will a hotter century demand?

Cooling degree days turn heat into potential energy demand. They estimate how much and how long outdoor temperatures sit above a comfort baseline. In the World Bank CCKP middle-road pathway, India's cooling load rises through the century, reaching roughly 6,100 degree-days by 2100. That is not a prediction of electricity use. Actual power demand depends on income, appliance ownership, building design, tariffs and whether power is reliable enough to run cooling when people need it. But the direction is the point. A hotter India will need more cooling. If that cooling is unequal, poorer households bear the health cost. If it is coal-heavy, the grid feeds the heat it is trying to escape.

## How to read these numbers

Most climate charts here use ERA5, a reanalysis that blends observations with model physics on a grid. It is not a thermometer at every home, and it should not be read as a district-level heat map. Temperature anomalies are measured against the 1991-2020 normal unless the source says otherwise. The hourly heat and rainfall metrics were derived locally from ERA5 hourly temperature, dew point and precipitation. The 2026 charts run only through May, so compare them only with January-May in earlier years. IMD provides the long observed monsoon check. CCKP projections are scenarios, not forecasts. Crop and food-price charts are stress tests, not proof of one-cause inflation. Cooling, work, vulnerability and mortality charts combine different survey, administrative and modelled sources; use them to understand exposure and uncertainty, not to pretend India has one perfect climate-risk number.

glossaryBlocks.definition: The difference between a year's temperature and a chosen normal period. Here, most ERA5 anomalies use 1991-2020.
A gridded climate estimate that blends observations with model physics. ERA5 is reanalysis, not a thermometer in every location.
A body-stress measure that combines temperature and humidity to estimate how hot conditions feel.

chartExplainers.visualId: India's climate line has moved
chartExplainers.title: India's climate line has moved
chartExplainers.takeaway: India is warmer than the recent normal, and the national average understates local heat.
chartExplainers.detail: Read the zero line as the 1991-2020 normal. Values above zero are warmer than that recent baseline; values below zero are cooler. ERA5 shows India moving from much cooler than the recent normal in the early record to mostly warmer in the latest decade. The exact annual decimal is less important than the shift in the whole distribution. A national annual anomaly is not the temperature anyone feels outside. It is the smoothed signal beneath hotter days, hotter nights, heavier cooling demand and more stressful monsoon risk.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This is the anchor chart. It answers whether the climate signal is real before the article moves into lived exposure.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Follow the line through time and compare early decades with the latest decade, not just the last point.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat a small decimal as a small lived change. A country-wide annual anomaly is a large average.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, focus first on the zero line and the recent cluster of points above it.

chartExplainers.visualId: Three datasets tell the same warming story
chartExplainers.title: Three datasets tell the same warming story
chartExplainers.takeaway: The India warming signal does not disappear when the source changes.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart rebases three independent temperature products to the same 1991-2020 normal so their direction can be compared. ERA5, OWID/Copernicus and Berkeley Earth do not produce identical annual values, and they should not be expected to: they use different methods, source inputs and land masks. The useful result is that the older decades sit lower and the recent decades sit higher across sources. That answers the cherry-picking objection before the article moves into heat, rain, work and health.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It separates the core warming signal from a fight over one dataset or one unusually hot year.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the broad movement of the three lines around the zero baseline, not tiny annual gaps between them.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat the three products as station thermometers measuring the same spot. Agreement on direction is the evidence here.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, use the legend and zero line first; the exact separation between lines matters less than their shared upward shift.

chartExplainers.visualId: India has warmed about as much as the world
chartExplainers.title: India has warmed about as much as the world
chartExplainers.takeaway: India is not uniquely fastest, but roughly one degree is not a small result.
chartExplainers.detail: Each bar compares a country or region's 2016-2025 average temperature anomaly with its 1940s average in the same OWID/Copernicus series. India is about 0.97°C warmer on this calculation, close to Bangladesh and the world total, below China and far below the United States in this selected set. This is the fair answer to the claim that India is not warming as fast: the claim is partly true if the question is ranking, but misleading if it is used to imply low risk. A national annual degree is a large average in a country already near dangerous heat thresholds.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It gives readers a clean cross-country benchmark without letting comparison erase exposure.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the bars as degrees Celsius warmer between two decade averages, not as a percentage and not as absolute temperature.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not infer lived risk from rank alone. Exposure, humidity, poverty, work patterns and cooling access decide how warming is felt.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, find India and the world bars first, then compare them with nearby countries and the higher-warming outliers.

chartExplainers.visualId: Every region is warming, but not the same way
chartExplainers.title: Every region is warming, but not the same way
chartExplainers.takeaway: India is not warming as one block.
chartExplainers.detail: The national line hides a rougher map. The Himalayan belt has warmed far faster than the all-India average in this ERA5 regional split, while the Indo-Gangetic plain, the arid west, the Deccan and the peninsula have their own rhythms. That does not mean the mountains are the only danger zone. High warming in a sparse mountain belt matters for snow, glaciers, springs and downstream water. The chart stops the all-India average from doing too much work.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The chart stops the all-India average from doing too much work.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare each line's early years with its recent years, then compare the regions with one another.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not read regional averages as city or district readings.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use the legend to isolate one or two regions if the lines feel dense.

chartExplainers.visualId: The warming map is uneven
chartExplainers.title: The warming map is uneven
chartExplainers.takeaway: State-level warming turns the climate story into an administrative problem.
chartExplainers.detail: The state map makes the same point in political geography. States are not climate zones, but they are where heat action plans, school closures, power supply and disaster relief get administered. A national average cannot tell a state government whether its problem is hot nights, dry pre-monsoon heat, humid coastal heat or flood bursts. The map also warns against a simple north-versus-south reading. People experience climate through local governments and local infrastructure, not an all-India mean.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: People experience climate through local governments and local infrastructure, not an all-India mean.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read darker shading as larger average warming, then remember population exposure can be high even in less dark states.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not rank exact risk from colour alone. Heat hazard and vulnerability are not the same thing.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, use the labels and the legend before comparing neighbouring states.

chartExplainers.visualId: The pre-monsoon heat window matters most
chartExplainers.title: The pre-monsoon heat window matters most
chartExplainers.takeaway: March-May heat carries more daily-life risk than the annual average suggests.
chartExplainers.detail: March to May is the dangerous waiting room before the monsoon. In the ERA5 pre-monsoon series, the latest decade sits above the 1991-2020 normal while older decades sit lower, and the peak years are much hotter than the average. That matters because this is when reservoirs are drawn down, construction and delivery work become harder, schools debate closures and power demand climbs before rain brings relief. The chart keeps the article from hiding a brutal season inside a tidy annual average.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The article needs a seasonal heat chart because annual averages can hide the months people fear most.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read it like the annual anomaly chart, but only for March-May.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not use it as a monsoon forecast. Heat before the monsoon and rain during the monsoon are linked in complex ways, not one simple rule.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare the recent decade with the 1980s rather than chasing every spike.

chartExplainers.visualId: 2026 so far belongs in its own box
chartExplainers.title: 2026 so far belongs in its own box
chartExplainers.takeaway: January-May 2026 is hot, but it is a partial-year comparison.
chartExplainers.detail: Through January-May, 2026 is hot, but the honest comparison is only against earlier January-May periods. In this ERA5 year-to-date series, all-India January-May 2026 is about 0.44°C above the 1991-2020 January-May normal. That ranks seventh warmest in the 1940-2026 comparable record, not first. The point is still important: current-year heat is already elevated, but the chart prevents a half-year result from being sold as a completed annual climate verdict.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Readers want a current-year answer; this chart gives it without abusing the data.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare like with like: January-May against January-May.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not compare 2026 YTD with completed calendar years.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, read the latest endpoint first, then scan how often earlier years reached similar levels.

chartExplainers.visualId: The nights are not cooling like they used to
chartExplainers.title: The nights are not cooling like they used to
chartExplainers.takeaway: Warm nights are one of the clearest lived heat signals.
chartExplainers.detail: Warm nights are the difference between a bad day and a bad week. In the hourly ERA5-derived series, all-India warm nights, when the regional daily minimum stays at or above 26°C, averaged about 47 nights a year in the 1980s. In 2016-2025, that average was roughly 74. The latest year, 2025, had about 68 such nights, down from the extreme 2024 peak but still far above the 1980s. Night-time heat connects climate directly to sleep, health and work capacity.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Night-time heat connects climate directly to sleep, health and work capacity.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the y-axis as nights per year. Compare decade averages, not only the latest point.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume a cooler latest year means the trend has vanished.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, the all-India and regional endpoint labels are the fastest read.

chartExplainers.visualId: The hottest days are a regional story
chartExplainers.title: The hottest days are a regional story
chartExplainers.takeaway: A 40°C threshold exposes regional heat that the national average can hide.
chartExplainers.detail: The 40°C chart is a useful trap for the eye because the all-India line does not rise neatly from left to right. Hot-day counts depend on geography, season and threshold: some regions are already so hot that the count behaves differently from a national temperature anomaly. This is why the article uses 40°C days as a lived-exposure metric, not as the master proof of climate change. The warming story is clearer in nights, humid heat and regional risk than in one hard daytime cutoff.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It prevents a false comfort from the annual-average line.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Track each region separately and look for the highest-exposure regions.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not conclude that heat risk is easing because the all-India 40°C count falls in one year.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, focus on the top line and the all-India line first.

chartExplainers.visualId: Humidity turns heat into body stress
chartExplainers.title: Humidity turns heat into body stress
chartExplainers.takeaway: Humid heat has risen more clearly than dry 40°C days.
chartExplainers.detail: Humidity is the reason two 38°C days can feel completely different. Sweat cools the body only when it evaporates. When the air is wet, evaporation slows and the same thermometer reading becomes harder to survive. In the hourly ERA5-derived heat-index series, all-India humid-heat days at or above a 40°C heat index averaged about 42 days a year in the 1980s. This is the bridge from thermometer heat to body stress.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: This is the bridge from thermometer heat to body stress.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read it as days per year of high heat-index exposure.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat heat index as a count of illness or deaths. It is an exposure proxy.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare the recent cluster of each line with the earliest decade.

chartExplainers.visualId: The monsoon has become a sharper risk
chartExplainers.title: The monsoon has become a sharper risk
chartExplainers.takeaway: The monsoon story is volatility, timing and intensity, not a smooth trend.
chartExplainers.detail: The monsoon chart should not be read as a neat warming line. Rain is noisier than temperature. The all-India southwest monsoon anomaly swings hard from year to year, with 1987 deeply dry and 2025 well above the 1991-2020 normal in ERA5. The latest decade in this series was wetter than the 1980s on average, but that is not the comfort it first sounds like. India's water and crop systems depend on the monsoon, so the article needs this spine.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: India's water and crop systems depend on the monsoon, so the article needs this spine.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read zero as the 1991-2020 monsoon normal and watch departures above or below it.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not use one wet year to dismiss climate risk.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, use the zero line and the largest dry/wet spikes as anchors.

chartExplainers.visualId: Rainy days are not moving together across India
chartExplainers.title: Rainy days are not moving together across India
chartExplainers.takeaway: Rain frequency is changing differently by region.
chartExplainers.detail: Wet-day counts ask a simple question the seasonal-total chart cannot: is rain spread out across usable days? In the ERA5 hourly-derived all-India series, days with at least 1 mm of regional-average rain averaged about 114 in the 1980s and about 125 in 2016-2025. The regional lines do not move in perfect lockstep. That matters because agriculture, groundwater recharge and city drainage care about sequencing. It adds a timing lens that total rainfall cannot provide.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It adds a timing lens that total rainfall cannot provide.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the lines as days per year, not rainfall amount.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume every district in a region got rain on the same days.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare all-India with one region at a time.

chartExplainers.visualId: Heavy-rain days are the drainage problem
chartExplainers.title: Heavy-rain days are the drainage problem
chartExplainers.takeaway: Heavy rain turns climate into infrastructure stress.
chartExplainers.detail: Heavy-rain days translate climate into infrastructure. In the all-India ERA5 hourly-derived series, days above 50 mm are not just a rainfall statistic; they are the kind of days that test drains, roads, embankments, crop fields and informal settlements. A national average still hides local cloudbursts, but it shows whether the water year is arriving in sharper bursts. Read this beside wet days and five-day maxima: fewer or similar rainy days can still produce more damaging rain if more water arrives at once.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It gives the rain act a lived urban and farm consequence.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read it as frequency of heavy-rain days, not total rainfall.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not mistake regional averages for cloudburst intensity at a single locality.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, look for the lines that sit consistently higher.

chartExplainers.visualId: The wettest five-day spell is getting heavier
chartExplainers.title: The wettest five-day spell is getting heavier
chartExplainers.takeaway: Clustered rain is a flood signal.
chartExplainers.detail: The wettest five-day spell is a better flood signal than the annual total. In the all-India ERA5 hourly-derived series, the rainiest five-day stretch averaged about 159 mm in the 1980s and about 174 mm in 2016-2025. In 2024 it crossed 200 mm, and 2025 was still around 179 mm. This is the kind of clustering that tests dams, drains, slopes and crop fields. Five-day rainfall connects better to flooding and crop damage than annual totals do.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Five-day rainfall connects better to flooding and crop damage than annual totals do.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the y-axis as millimetres in the wettest five-day window each year.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not over-interpret a single spike.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare the early and late clusters rather than every year.

chartExplainers.visualId: The monsoon still carries most of the year's rain
chartExplainers.title: The monsoon still carries most of the year's rain
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's water year still depends heavily on June-September.
chartExplainers.detail: Even with changing seasons, the southwest monsoon still carries most of India's annual rain. In the hourly-derived ERA5 series, June-September usually supplies roughly seven-tenths to four-fifths of the year's precipitation. The latest decade averaged about 74%, close to the 1980s but with plenty of annual variation. This concentration is why the monsoon is not just weather. It explains why four months dominate water, farming and flood risk.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It explains why four months dominate water, farming and flood risk.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read it as a share of annual rainfall, not a measure of whether the monsoon was good.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not call a stable share safe. Timing and intensity still decide damage.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, focus on the band in which most years sit.

chartExplainers.visualId: IMD's long monsoon record shows why averages mislead
chartExplainers.title: IMD's long monsoon record shows why averages mislead
chartExplainers.takeaway: The observed monsoon record shows long-run volatility.
chartExplainers.detail: ERA5 gives a gridded climate spine. IMD's long all-India monsoon record is the historical reality check. It runs back to 1901 and shows why Indians have always treated the monsoon as a risk, not a tap. The worst drought years are deep, and the wettest years are not automatically good news because rain can arrive in destructive bursts. It checks the ERA5 rain story against India's observed monsoon history.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It checks the ERA5 rain story against India's observed monsoon history.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read departures from normal, not absolute rainfall.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not infer district floods or droughts from an all-India line.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, scan the largest negative and positive bars or points.

chartExplainers.visualId: 2026 is hot and drier so far, but only through May
chartExplainers.title: 2026 is hot and drier so far, but only through May
chartExplainers.takeaway: 2026 began dry as well as hot, but the monsoon verdict is open.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart gives the water counterpart to the 2026 heat box. ERA5 shows January-May 2026 on the drier side of the comparable record, but January-May is not the southwest monsoon and cannot by itself define a drought year. The value of the chart is discipline: it lets readers see why the year has felt stressed without pretending the main rainy season has already happened. The monsoon charts later in the article carry the real water-year test.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It gives the current-year box a water counterpart to the heat chart.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare January-May 2026 only with January-May in previous years.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not call 2026 a drought from this chart.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, read the latest endpoint and then the range of previous dry starts.

chartExplainers.visualId: Groundwater stress makes weak rain harder to absorb
chartExplainers.title: Groundwater stress makes weak rain harder to absorb
chartExplainers.takeaway: Groundwater decides how quickly a rainfall shock becomes a household shock.
chartExplainers.detail: Rainfall is the supply shock; groundwater is the buffer. When extraction is high relative to recharge, a weak monsoon reaches farms, taps and tankers faster because stored water cannot cushion the miss. The CGWB stage-of-extraction series is therefore not a separate water-policy tangent. It explains why the same rainfall anomaly can mean inconvenience in one place and distress in another. Climate risk is mediated by stored water, irrigation, local aquifers and the political capacity to move water where it is needed.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Climate risk is mediated by stored water, not just sky water.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read values near 100% as extraction close to annual recharge.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat this as a monthly water-table reading.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare the national line with the high-stress state examples.

chartExplainers.visualId: The sea is rising on India's coasts
chartExplainers.title: The sea is rising on India's coasts
chartExplainers.takeaway: Coastal climate risk comes from rain above and sea level at the edge.
chartExplainers.detail: For coastal India, climate change is not only heat and rain. A higher sea raises the floor under storm surge, high tides and drainage failure. The Mumbai and Chennai tide-gauge records are not perfect national sea-level measures. They combine ocean change with local land movement, and the histories have gaps. Coastal India needs a different hazard lens from inland heat.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Coastal India needs a different hazard lens from inland heat.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the direction and broad scale rather than any one annual point.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat tide gauges as a clean all-India sea-level average.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare each city with its own baseline, not with the other city point by point.

chartExplainers.visualId: The monsoon still shows up in the harvest
chartExplainers.title: The monsoon still shows up in the harvest
chartExplainers.takeaway: The monsoon still reaches the food system.
chartExplainers.detail: Irrigation, procurement and better seeds have weakened the old drought-to-famine chain. They have not made the monsoon irrelevant. The crop correlation chart shows which outputs still move with monsoon rainfall in the historical panel: foodgrains, rice and oilseeds track rainfall more than irrigated winter crops such as wheat. Treat it as a sensitivity map, not a one-cause explanation. Prices, procurement, acreage, pests, imports and policy still matter, but climate stress enters the food system through the crops that remain rain-sensitive.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It connects rain to agriculture without claiming rain explains everything.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read longer bars as stronger historical co-movement.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not call correlation causation.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare the longest and shortest bars first.

chartExplainers.visualId: Rainfed crops take the climate hit first
chartExplainers.title: Rainfed crops take the climate hit first
chartExplainers.takeaway: Weak-monsoon stress lands unevenly across crops.
chartExplainers.detail: The crop-yield stress test makes the food story more concrete. El Nino years are used here as weak-monsoon stress years, and each crop is compared with its own recent five-year normal. Rainfed kharif crops are more exposed than crops protected by irrigation or winter timing. That does not mean every El Nino year causes the same harvest loss. It shows why climate reaches the plate through specific crops, not food in general.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shows why climate reaches the plate through specific crops, not food in general.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read values as deviations from each crop's recent normal.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not compare bare percentages without remembering each crop has its own baseline.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, focus on which crops are below their normal.

chartExplainers.visualId: Climate shocks reach the plate unevenly
chartExplainers.title: Climate shocks reach the plate unevenly
chartExplainers.takeaway: Food prices respond through commodities, stocks and policy, not rainfall alone.
chartExplainers.detail: Food inflation is not one object. Cereals, pulses, onions, vegetables, edible oils and milk sit inside different supply chains. The food WPI component chart uses selected El Nino drought years to show why a weak monsoon does not produce one clean price response. Public grain stocks can soften cereals while pulses or onions jump. It stops a one-cause food-inflation story.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It stops a one-cause food-inflation story.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read each food group separately.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume a weak monsoon automatically raises every food price.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare the biggest food-group bars rather than the whole table at once.

chartExplainers.visualId: PM2.5 is still many times the safe-air guideline
chartExplainers.title: PM2.5 is still many times the safe-air guideline
chartExplainers.takeaway: Air pollution has improved in this series but remains severe.
chartExplainers.detail: PM2.5 is not climate change. It is dirty air. It belongs here because in India the lived exposure story overlaps: fossil-fuel combustion, crop-residue burning, dust, heat, stagnant air and weak household protection often hit the same people. The chart should not be read as a warming metric, but as context for the body that has to endure warming. Heat stress is harder when lungs and hearts are already strained by chronic air pollution, and many mitigation choices affect both carbon and particles.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Dirty air is a lived fossil-fuel exposure alongside climate warming.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read it as annual concentration in micrograms per cubic metre.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat it as a district-level or perfectly population-weighted estimate.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare the first and latest points.

chartExplainers.visualId: India's emissions are rising because development is energy-hungry
chartExplainers.title: India's emissions are rising because development is energy-hungry
chartExplainers.takeaway: India is exposed to warming and is also a growing annual emitter.
chartExplainers.detail: India's climate position is uncomfortable because two statements are true at once. The country is highly exposed to warming, and its annual CO2 emissions are still rising as electricity, transport, construction and industry grow. Development is energy-hungry. More homes want cooling, more factories need power, more cities move people and goods. The article must include cause as well as impact.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The article must include cause as well as impact.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the line as total national emissions.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not use total emissions alone to judge responsibility across countries of very different population sizes.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, focus on the long upward movement.

chartExplainers.visualId: Per person, India is still far below rich-country emissions
chartExplainers.title: Per person, India is still far below rich-country emissions
chartExplainers.takeaway: Per person is the fairness lens.
chartExplainers.detail: Per-person emissions are the fairness check. India has a large and rising national total because 1.4 billion people add up, but the average Indian still emits far less CO2 each year than the average person in the United States, China or many rich economies. This chart keeps two ideas in view at once: India matters for future global emissions, and India is not rich-country-style high emitting on a per-person basis. A serious climate article has to hold both without using one to erase the other.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It keeps the responsibility discussion honest.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare bar heights, not national totals.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not let per-person emissions erase the rising total, or total emissions erase the per-person gap.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, read India's bar against the world and US bars first.

chartExplainers.visualId: Where the emissions come from
chartExplainers.title: Where the emissions come from
chartExplainers.takeaway: Emissions are a work list, not one pipe.
chartExplainers.detail: The sector chart turns a moral argument into a work list. Electricity and heat, agriculture, manufacturing, transport, buildings, industry, waste and fugitive emissions are different problems. A coal power plant, paddy methane, a cement kiln and diesel freight do not have one solution. That is why a climate article needs sector composition after the total-emissions line. It gives the mitigation section structure.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It gives the mitigation section structure.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the largest slices first.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not turn sector share into a policy ranking by itself.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, use the legend and the largest blocks.

chartExplainers.visualId: The grid is changing, but coal still does the work
chartExplainers.title: The grid is changing, but coal still does the work
chartExplainers.takeaway: Clean power is rising, but coal remains the backbone.
chartExplainers.detail: India's electricity transition is real and incomplete. Ember's generation data shows solar and wind rising from a small base, while coal still supplies the largest block of electricity. That matters because the same warming that raises cooling demand also pushes up power demand. If the extra demand is met mainly by coal, cooling becomes an adaptation that feeds the problem. The grid links climate cause and climate coping.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The grid links climate cause and climate coping.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read generation in TWh, not installed capacity.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not assume capacity additions equal electricity generated.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare coal with solar and wind after locating the latest year.

chartExplainers.visualId: Cooling demand rises faster than cooling access
chartExplainers.title: Cooling demand rises faster than cooling access
chartExplainers.takeaway: The ability to escape heat is unequal.
chartExplainers.detail: Heat becomes inequality when the escape route is expensive. The cooling-access series show that only a small minority of Indian households had an air conditioner in the latest survey snapshot, with urban ownership far above rural ownership. NFHS and NSS measures are not a perfect annual time series, and appliance markets move faster than surveys. Still, the gap is the point. Cooling is the household face of adaptation.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Cooling is the household face of adaptation.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the lines as survey shares, not precise annual market sales.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not compare tiny changes across survey instruments too literally.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, focus on rural versus urban separation.

chartExplainers.visualId: The cooling map does not match the heat map
chartExplainers.title: The cooling map does not match the heat map
chartExplainers.takeaway: Cheap cooling works differently by climate.
chartExplainers.detail: Air coolers are common where dry heat makes them useful and cheaper than AC. They are much less useful in humid heat, where evaporation does not work well. That is why the cooler map should not be read as a simple protection map. High cooler ownership in dry states can still leave people exposed during very hot spells, and low ownership in humid states can reflect both poverty and the technology's limits. It explains why adaptation technology is geographic.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It explains why adaptation technology is geographic.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read darker states as higher air-cooler ownership.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat coolers as equivalent to AC.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare broad regional patterns rather than exact borders.

chartExplainers.visualId: Where heat is hardest to survive
chartExplainers.title: Where heat is hardest to survive
chartExplainers.takeaway: Heat vulnerability is hazard plus ability to cope.
chartExplainers.detail: The vulnerability scatter joins three things often discussed separately: heat risk, lack of cooling protection and poverty. The dangerous corner is not simply the hottest state. It is the place where high heat exposure meets households without reliable cooling and less money to adapt. This is not a mortality model and it should not be read as a precise ranking of deaths. It is a pressure map for policy: heat action, power reliability, housing quality and income support matter most where exposure and low coping capacity overlap.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It joins climate data to social inequality.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read rightward as more heat-risk districts and upward as less cooling protection.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not rank exact mortality risk from this chart.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, identify the upper-right cluster first.

chartExplainers.visualId: Heat hits work before it hits GDP tables
chartExplainers.title: Heat hits work before it hits GDP tables
chartExplainers.takeaway: Heat exposure sits heavily on outdoor and insecure work.
chartExplainers.detail: India still has a large share of workers in agriculture and other vulnerable work. That exposure matters because heat first shows up as shorter work windows, slower pace, more breaks, higher illness risk and lost daily wages. GDP tables see some of that late, and some not at all. A salaried office worker with AC can shift hours or work indoors. It connects climate to livelihoods.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It connects climate to livelihoods.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the chart as workforce exposure over time.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not call it a measured heat-damage series.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare the latest level with the older high-employment period.

chartExplainers.visualId: Heat is already costing work hours
chartExplainers.title: Heat is already costing work hours
chartExplainers.takeaway: Outdoor sectors carry most estimated heat-related labour loss.
chartExplainers.detail: The Lancet Countdown labour-loss chart moves from exposure to estimated loss. In its India data sheet, agriculture accounts for about 66% of heat-related labour-hour losses and construction for about 20%. The underlying estimate is about 247 billion potential labour hours lost in 2024, not a payroll record and not a count of people absent from work. It is a modelled labour-capacity measure based on heat stress. It moves from exposure to estimated economic burden.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It moves from exposure to estimated economic burden.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the bars as shares of heat-related labour-hour loss.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not treat them as observed absences or wage losses.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, the two largest bars carry the message.

chartExplainers.visualId: Heat deaths depend on how you count them
chartExplainers.title: Heat deaths depend on how you count them
chartExplainers.takeaway: Heat mortality is definition-sensitive.
chartExplainers.detail: Heat mortality is where bad counting can become bad policy. Certified heatstroke deaths, disaster databases, surveillance reports and modelled excess deaths answer different questions. The small administrative counts depend on diagnosis, death certification and reporting channels. The large modelled estimates try to capture deaths that rise during heat even when the certificate does not say "heatstroke". The chart prevents false certainty about the human toll.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: The chart prevents false certainty about the human toll.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read each bar with its source family and evidence type.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not rank the bars as if they measure the same thing.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, use the labels carefully because the scale spans very different counts.

chartExplainers.visualId: A hotter century means more cooling load
chartExplainers.title: A hotter century means more cooling load
chartExplainers.takeaway: Future cooling need rises under warming scenarios.
chartExplainers.detail: Cooling degree days turn heat into potential energy demand. They estimate how much and how long outdoor temperatures sit above a comfort baseline. In the World Bank CCKP middle-road pathway, India's cooling load rises through the century, reaching roughly 6,100 degree-days by 2100. That is not a prediction of electricity use. It closes the loop between future heat, bills and the grid.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It closes the loop between future heat, bills and the grid.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the scenario lines as pathways, not forecasts.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not confuse potential demand with actual electricity consumption.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: On mobile, compare the late-century spread across scenarios.

sourceNotes: Copernicus ERA5 reanalysis: monthly and hourly 2m temperature, dew point and precipitation fields processed locally for India, states and broad regions. Most anomalies use a 1991-2020 baseline.

OWID annual temperature anomalies and Berkeley Earth: used to compare India's warming signal across independent temperature products and selected countries; decade averages are used to avoid over-reading a single hot or cool year.
India Meteorological Department: long all-India southwest monsoon rainfall departure record used as the observed check beside ERA5 rainfall.
Central Ground Water Board and Permanent Service for Mean Sea Level: groundwater extraction-stage accounts and tide-gauge records used for water-buffer and coastal-risk context.
Agriculture and price context: crop-rainfall and El Nino stress-test series derived from Indian agricultural production datasets, with post-monsoon food WPI components from RBI wholesale-price data.
IQAir: annual country-average PM2.5 concentration for recent air-quality context. It depends on monitor coverage and is not a perfect population-weighted exposure estimate.
OWID, Global Carbon Project, Climate Watch/Data Commons and Ember: CO2, greenhouse-gas sector composition and electricity-generation series used for responsibility and transition context.
NSS, NFHS, NITI Aayog, CEEW, PLFS, ILO and Lancet Countdown: household cooling, poverty, heat-risk, employment exposure and heat-related labour-hour loss context.
World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal: cooling-degree-day scenarios used only as future pathways, not forecasts.
caveats: A positive anomaly means warmer than the chosen baseline, not warmer than a pre-industrial climate. Most ERA5 charts here use 1991-2020.
Cross-country warming comparisons here are anomaly differences between decade averages. They are degrees Celsius, not percentages, and they are not a ranking of lived climate risk.
Temperature anomaly products use different baselines, methods and source data. Re-basing helps compare direction; it does not make tiny annual gaps between products meaningful.
ERA5 is reanalysis. It gives consistent gridded estimates, but local stations, dense city streets, tin-roof homes and worksites can differ sharply from the grid average.
The hourly heat and rainfall metrics are derived locally from ERA5 hourly temperature, dew point and precipitation. They are exposure metrics, not health outcomes or flood-loss estimates.
The 2026 charts cover January-May only. They must be compared with January-May in earlier years, not with completed calendar years or a finished monsoon.
Rainfall totals, wet-day counts and heavy-rain thresholds are regional averages. They can understate local cloudbursts, dry spells and district-level flood damage.
Crop and food-price charts are stress tests and correlations. They do not prove a single causal path from climate to harvest or inflation.
Cooling-access data come from survey vintages that lag the market. Ownership does not guarantee affordable cooling during long heatwaves or power cuts.

Mortality, labour-loss and vulnerability charts combine administrative, survey and modelled sources. Use them to understand scale and uncertainty, not to pretend there is one exact climate-risk number.

plannedCharts.title: India's climate line has moved
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The core answer: the national climate is warmer than the recent normal, not just in one bad summer.

plannedCharts.title: Three datasets tell the same warming story
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This answers the cherry-picking objection: the warming signal is not a quirk of one dataset.

plannedCharts.title: India has warmed about as much as the world
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This answers the 'India is not warming fast' claim with a fair cross-country comparison.

plannedCharts.title: Every region is warming, but not the same way
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The national average hides different regional climates and different lived risks.

plannedCharts.title: The warming map is uneven
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: People live in states, not in an all-India average, and warming has not landed evenly.

plannedCharts.title: The pre-monsoon heat window matters most
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: March-May is when heat stress peaks before rain relief arrives, so seasonal warming matters more than annual warming alone.

plannedCharts.title: 2026 so far belongs in its own box
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The current year is a live hook, but partial years must be compared only with the same months in earlier years.

plannedCharts.title: The nights are not cooling like they used to
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Warm nights are what make heat hard to recover from: the body, the house and the city never get a proper reset.

plannedCharts.title: The hottest days are a regional story
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A national annual average cannot tell a farmer in Rajasthan or a street vendor in Delhi how many punishing days they face.

plannedCharts.title: Humidity turns heat into body stress
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The danger is not only thermometer heat. Humidity decides whether sweat can cool the body.

plannedCharts.title: The monsoon has become a sharper risk
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India does not live on annual rainfall alone. It lives on whether the monsoon arrives, pauses, dumps or fails.

plannedCharts.title: Rainy days are not moving together across India
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Annual rain totals miss whether rain is spread across usable days or squeezed into fewer bursts.

plannedCharts.title: Heavy-rain days are the drainage problem
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The lived rain risk is often an overloaded drain, a flooded road or a crop field waterlogged in one spell.

plannedCharts.title: The wettest five-day spell is getting heavier
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Reservoirs, drains and fields feel clustered rain, not just seasonal totals.

plannedCharts.title: The monsoon still carries most of the year's rain
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The monsoon matters because so much of India's annual water arrives in one season.

plannedCharts.title: IMD's long monsoon record shows why averages mislead
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: ERA5 gives the gridded climate layer; IMD's observed monsoon record is the historical reality check.

plannedCharts.title: 2026 is hot and drier so far, but only through May
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The current-year section should show heat and rainfall together, while being explicit that the monsoon is not complete.

plannedCharts.title: Groundwater stress makes weak rain harder to absorb
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Climate risk is not only how much rain falls. It is also whether farms and cities have a water buffer when rain fails or arrives badly.

plannedCharts.title: The sea is rising on India's coasts
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: For coastal cities, climate change is not only a hot-day problem. Higher seas raise the floor under storm surge, drainage failure and chronic flooding.

plannedCharts.title: The monsoon still shows up in the harvest
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The rain story becomes a household story through crops. Even after irrigation and technology gains, monsoon rainfall is still visible in output.

plannedCharts.title: Rainfed crops take the climate hit first
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Climate damage is not evenly spread across the plate. Rainfed kharif crops are more exposed than irrigated or winter crops.

plannedCharts.title: Climate shocks reach the plate unevenly
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Food inflation is not one number in lived experience. A weak monsoon can leave cereals buffered while pulses, onions or vegetables do the damage.

plannedCharts.title: PM2.5 is still many times the safe-air guideline
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The live AQI snapshot needs a recent annual PM2.5 measure beside it, not a stale World Bank series ending in 2020.

plannedCharts.title: India's emissions are rising because development is energy-hungry
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The country is both exposed to warming and a growing contributor to the cause.

plannedCharts.title: Per person, India is still far below rich-country emissions
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A fair climate article has to hold scale and responsibility together.

plannedCharts.title: Where the emissions come from
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The solution set depends on the source: power, farms, industry and transport are different problems.

plannedCharts.title: The grid is changing, but coal still does the work
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: India's climate path turns heavily on whether clean electricity grows faster than demand.

plannedCharts.title: Cooling demand rises faster than cooling access
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Heat becomes inequality when the escape route is an appliance most households do not have.

plannedCharts.title: The cooling map does not match the heat map
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The appliance people can afford is not always the appliance the climate needs. Evaporative coolers are common in the dry north and weak in humid heat.

plannedCharts.title: Where heat is hardest to survive
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: A climate impact article needs to join hazard with the ability to cope. The dangerous zone is high heat risk, low cooling protection and poverty together.

plannedCharts.title: Heat hits work before it hits GDP tables
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Outdoor and insecure work turns climate from a weather story into an income story.

plannedCharts.title: Heat is already costing work hours
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: This moves from exposure to measured economic loss: heat already cuts labour capacity, especially in outdoor sectors.

plannedCharts.title: Heat deaths depend on how you count them
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: The mortality record is part of the climate story because official heatstroke counts and modelled excess deaths answer different questions.

plannedCharts.title: A hotter century means more cooling load
plannedCharts.whyThisChart: Cooling is the bridge between climate, household bills and the power grid.
