selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.

visualPlan.title: India's climate line has moved
visualPlan.why: The core answer: the national climate is warmer than the recent normal, not just in one bad summer.
visualPlan.read: Each point is India's annual mean temperature anomaly from ERA5, compared with the 1991-2020 average. Positive years are hotter than the recent normal.
visualPlan.watch: This is a national annual average. It smooths out the heat that people feel in particular weeks, cities and worksites.

visualPlan.title: Three datasets tell the same warming story
visualPlan.why: This answers the cherry-picking objection: the warming signal is not a quirk of one dataset.
visualPlan.read: Three independent India temperature-anomaly series are rebased to the same 1991-2020 normal so the direction can be compared.
visualPlan.watch: The lines will not match exactly because sources, land masks and methods differ. Agreement on direction matters more than tiny annual gaps.

visualPlan.title: India has warmed about as much as the world
visualPlan.why: This answers the 'India is not warming fast' claim with a fair cross-country comparison.
visualPlan.read: Each bar compares the average annual temperature anomaly in 2016-2025 with the 1940s average for that country or region.
visualPlan.watch: This is a change in temperature anomaly, not a percent. A roughly one-degree national shift is not small in a hot, humid, populous country.

visualPlan.title: Every region is warming, but not the same way
visualPlan.why: The national average hides different regional climates and different lived risks.
visualPlan.read: Each line is a broad Indian region's ERA5 annual temperature anomaly from the same 1991-2020 baseline.
visualPlan.watch: Regions are broad state groupings. They explain scale better than a national average, but they still hide city and district extremes.

visualPlan.title: The warming map is uneven
visualPlan.why: People live in states, not in an all-India average, and warming has not landed evenly.
visualPlan.read: Each state is shaded by how much its average temperature rose, comparing 2015-2024 against the 1951-1980 baseline. Darker means more warming.
visualPlan.watch: State averages still smooth over cities, valleys and coastlines. Mountain states often warm faster, but dense plains carry the larger population exposure.

visualPlan.title: The pre-monsoon heat window matters most
visualPlan.why: March-May is when heat stress peaks before rain relief arrives, so seasonal warming matters more than annual warming alone.
visualPlan.read: ERA5 March-May temperature anomaly for all India, compared with 1991-2020.
visualPlan.watch: A hot pre-monsoon season does not automatically predict the monsoon. It is a heat-exposure measure, not a rainfall forecast.

visualPlan.title: 2026 so far belongs in its own box
visualPlan.why: The current year is a live hook, but partial years must be compared only with the same months in earlier years.
visualPlan.read: Each line compares January-May temperature in every year with the January-May 1991-2020 normal. The latest point is 2026 through May.
visualPlan.watch: Do not rank 2026 against full calendar years. This is a year-to-date comparison through May only.

visualPlan.title: The nights are not cooling like they used to
visualPlan.why: Warm nights are what make heat hard to recover from: the body, the house and the city never get a proper reset.
visualPlan.read: Hourly ERA5 temperatures are converted into daily minimums, then counted as warm nights when the minimum stays at or above 26°C.
visualPlan.watch: This is region-average exposure. A city neighbourhood or a tin-roofed room can be worse than the grid-cell average.

visualPlan.title: The hottest days are a regional story
visualPlan.why: A national annual average cannot tell a farmer in Rajasthan or a street vendor in Delhi how many punishing days they face.
visualPlan.read: Hourly ERA5 temperatures are converted to daily maximums. Each line counts days when the maximum reached at least 40°C.
visualPlan.watch: Threshold days can fall in a cooler year if the heat was short and sharp. Use this with the anomaly charts, not instead of them.

visualPlan.title: Humidity turns heat into body stress
visualPlan.why: The danger is not only thermometer heat. Humidity decides whether sweat can cool the body.
visualPlan.read: Hourly ERA5 temperature and dew point are used to calculate heat index. A day counts when the daily maximum heat index reaches at least 40°C.
visualPlan.watch: Heat index is a body-stress proxy, not a medical outcome. It says exposure rose, not how many people fell sick.

visualPlan.title: The monsoon has become a sharper risk
visualPlan.why: India does not live on annual rainfall alone. It lives on whether the monsoon arrives, pauses, dumps or fails.
visualPlan.read: ERA5 June-September precipitation anomaly for all India, compared with 1991-2020.
visualPlan.watch: A national monsoon total hides dry spells, floods and regional failures. Timing can hurt even when the season total looks normal.

visualPlan.title: Rainy days are not moving together across India
visualPlan.why: Annual rain totals miss whether rain is spread across usable days or squeezed into fewer bursts.
visualPlan.read: ERA5 hourly precipitation is summed to daily rainfall. A wet day is counted when the regional daily total reaches at least 1 mm.
visualPlan.watch: This is a regional-average wet-day count. It does not say that every district got rain on the same days.

visualPlan.title: Heavy-rain days are the drainage problem
visualPlan.why: The lived rain risk is often an overloaded drain, a flooded road or a crop field waterlogged in one spell.
visualPlan.read: A heavy-rain day is counted when ERA5-derived daily precipitation reaches at least 50 mm in the regional average.
visualPlan.watch: A regional average mutes local cloudbursts. District-level flood risk can be worse than this line looks.

visualPlan.title: The wettest five-day spell is getting heavier
visualPlan.why: Reservoirs, drains and fields feel clustered rain, not just seasonal totals.
visualPlan.read: For each year, this picks the rainiest five-day stretch in each region from ERA5 hourly-derived daily rainfall.
visualPlan.watch: The line is an annual maximum, so it is naturally jumpy. Read the decade-level shift, not one spike.

visualPlan.title: The monsoon still carries most of the year's rain
visualPlan.why: The monsoon matters because so much of India's annual water arrives in one season.
visualPlan.read: Share of annual ERA5 hourly-derived precipitation falling in June-September.
visualPlan.watch: A stable or rising share does not mean the monsoon is safe. Timing, region and intensity still decide damage.

visualPlan.title: IMD's long monsoon record shows why averages mislead
visualPlan.why: ERA5 gives the gridded climate layer; IMD's observed monsoon record is the historical reality check.
visualPlan.read: All-India southwest monsoon rainfall departure from the long-period average, 1901-2025.
visualPlan.watch: This is all-India rainfall. It does not say which district flooded or failed in a given year.

visualPlan.title: 2026 is hot and drier so far, but only through May
visualPlan.why: The current-year section should show heat and rainfall together, while being explicit that the monsoon is not complete.
visualPlan.read: Each line compares January-May precipitation with the same-month 1991-2020 normal. The latest point is 2026 through May.
visualPlan.watch: This is before the full southwest monsoon. It is not a verdict on 2026 rainfall.

visualPlan.title: Groundwater stress makes weak rain harder to absorb
visualPlan.why: Climate risk is not only how much rain falls. It is also whether farms and cities have a water buffer when rain fails or arrives badly.
visualPlan.read: CGWB stage of groundwater extraction compares annual extraction with extractable groundwater resource. Values near or above 100% mean extraction is close to or above the assessed rechargeable resource.
visualPlan.watch: These are assessment-cycle groundwater accounts, not monthly aquifer levels. They do not capture every local well or urban tanker market.

visualPlan.title: The sea is rising on India's coasts
visualPlan.why: For coastal cities, climate change is not only a hot-day problem. Higher seas raise the floor under storm surge, drainage failure and chronic flooding.
visualPlan.read: Permanent Service for Mean Sea Level tide-gauge series, expressed relative to the 1961-1990 average.
visualPlan.watch: Tide gauges combine ocean change with local land movement and have gaps. Use the direction and scale, not a single annual point.

visualPlan.title: The monsoon still shows up in the harvest
visualPlan.why: The rain story becomes a household story through crops. Even after irrigation and technology gains, monsoon rainfall is still visible in output.
visualPlan.read: Bars show the correlation between monsoon rainfall and crop output in the DES panel. Higher bars mean crop output tracks the monsoon more closely.
visualPlan.watch: Correlation is not causation. Crop prices, area, irrigation, procurement, seed technology and heat all move output too.

visualPlan.title: Rainfed crops take the climate hit first
visualPlan.why: Climate damage is not evenly spread across the plate. Rainfed kharif crops are more exposed than irrigated or winter crops.
visualPlan.read: Each bar shows how far that crop's national yield ran from its own recent five-year average in El Nino years.
visualPlan.watch: This uses El Nino years as a stress-test for weak monsoon risk. It is not a full model of every climate pathway.

visualPlan.title: Climate shocks reach the plate unevenly
visualPlan.why: Food inflation is not one number in lived experience. A weak monsoon can leave cereals buffered while pulses, onions or vegetables do the damage.
visualPlan.read: Bars split post-monsoon wholesale inflation by food group in selected El Nino drought years.
visualPlan.watch: Prices answer to stocks, imports, procurement and global markets as well as rain. Do not read this as a one-cause inflation model.

visualPlan.title: PM2.5 is still many times the safe-air guideline
visualPlan.why: The live AQI snapshot needs a recent annual PM2.5 measure beside it, not a stale World Bank series ending in 2020.
visualPlan.read: IQAir annual country-average PM2.5 concentration, in micrograms per cubic metre, 2018-2025.
visualPlan.watch: This is monitor-network coverage, not a perfectly population-weighted exposure estimate. Use it for recent national air-quality context, not district-level exposure.

visualPlan.title: India's emissions are rising because development is energy-hungry
visualPlan.why: The country is both exposed to warming and a growing contributor to the cause.
visualPlan.read: Annual CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and cement.
visualPlan.watch: Total emissions are not the fairness number. Use them with per-person and historical comparisons.

visualPlan.title: Per person, India is still far below rich-country emissions
visualPlan.why: A fair climate article has to hold scale and responsibility together.
visualPlan.read: Latest CO2 per person for India, China, the United States and the world average.
visualPlan.watch: Per-person emissions do not erase India's rising total, and total emissions do not erase the per-person gap.

visualPlan.title: Where the emissions come from
visualPlan.why: The solution set depends on the source: power, farms, industry and transport are different problems.
visualPlan.read: Latest sector composition of greenhouse gas emissions, in CO2-equivalent.
visualPlan.watch: This is composition, not a policy scorecard. It says where emissions sit, not which intervention is easiest.

visualPlan.title: The grid is changing, but coal still does the work
visualPlan.why: India's climate path turns heavily on whether clean electricity grows faster than demand.
visualPlan.read: Annual electricity generation by source. Coal remains the largest line while solar and wind rise from a low base.
visualPlan.watch: Generation is not capacity. A gigawatt of solar and a gigawatt of coal do not produce the same annual electricity.

visualPlan.title: Cooling demand rises faster than cooling access
visualPlan.why: Heat becomes inequality when the escape route is an appliance most households do not have.
visualPlan.read: Household cooling ownership measures from NSS/NFHS-derived artifacts.
visualPlan.watch: These are survey snapshots from different instruments, not a perfect annual time series. Read the rural-urban gap more than tiny differences.

visualPlan.title: The cooling map does not match the heat map
visualPlan.why: The appliance people can afford is not always the appliance the climate needs. Evaporative coolers are common in the dry north and weak in humid heat.
visualPlan.read: Each state is shaded by the share of households owning an air cooler in NSS 78.
visualPlan.watch: Coolers are not air conditioners. Low ownership in humid states reflects both affordability and the fact that coolers work poorly in damp air.

visualPlan.title: Where heat is hardest to survive
visualPlan.why: A climate impact article needs to join hazard with the ability to cope. The dangerous zone is high heat risk, low cooling protection and poverty together.
visualPlan.read: Right means more districts rated high or very high heat risk. Up means more households without the conservative cooling-protection proxy. Bigger bubbles are poorer states.
visualPlan.watch: This is not a death-risk model. It combines state-level context from different sources, so use it to locate vulnerability, not to rank exact mortality risk.

visualPlan.title: Heat hits work before it hits GDP tables
visualPlan.why: Outdoor and insecure work turns climate from a weather story into an income story.
visualPlan.read: Shares of employment in agriculture and vulnerable work, both exposed to heat and rainfall disruption.
visualPlan.watch: These series show exposure, not measured heat damages. They say who is in harm's way, not exactly how much income was lost.

visualPlan.title: Heat is already costing work hours
visualPlan.why: This moves from exposure to measured economic loss: heat already cuts labour capacity, especially in outdoor sectors.
visualPlan.read: Bars split heat-related labour-hour losses by sector in Lancet Countdown's India data sheet.
visualPlan.watch: These are shares of estimated heat-related labour-hour losses, not observed absences or wages.

visualPlan.title: Heat deaths depend on how you count them
visualPlan.why: The mortality record is part of the climate story because official heatstroke counts and modelled excess deaths answer different questions.
visualPlan.read: Bars compare administrative, disaster, surveillance and modelled estimates on a log scale, using each source's own definition.
visualPlan.watch: Do not rank these as rival measurements of one fact. The large estimates are modelled excess mortality; the smaller ones are reported or certified counts.

visualPlan.title: A hotter century means more cooling load
visualPlan.why: Cooling is the bridge between climate, household bills and the power grid.
visualPlan.read: Cooling degree days estimate how much and how long temperatures exceed a comfort baseline.
visualPlan.watch: This is potential cooling demand. Actual electricity use depends on income, housing, appliance access and power reliability.
